blocks.text: E standard values give the voltage of an electrochemical cell made from two half-cells even when neither is a standard hydrogen electrode: the voltage measured is the difference between the E standard values of the two half-cells, called the standard cell potential, E cell. For the cell of Figure 10.8, the half-equations are Ag+(aq) + e- giving Ag(s), E standard = +0.80 V, and Zn2+(aq) + 2e- giving Zn(s), E standard = -0.76 V, so the voltage is +0.80 - (-0.76) = +1.56 V. The E standard value of the Ag+/Ag half-cell is more positive than that of the Zn2+/Zn half-cell, so the Ag+/Ag half-cell is the positive pole and the Zn2+/Zn half-cell the negative pole.

blocks.alt: (a) Two half-cells joined by a salt bridge at 298 K: a silver rod marked Ag in Ag+ (1 mol/dm3), terminal +, and a zinc rod marked Zn in Zn2+ (1 mol/dm3), terminal -, wired to a voltmeter reading 1.56 V; arrows on the wire run from zinc to silver, e- marked at both ends. (b) An E-standard scale from +1.00 to -1.00 with Ag+ + e- in equilibrium with Ag at +0.80 V (red) and Zn2+ + 2e- in equilibrium with Zn at -0.76 V (blue), joined by a double arrow marked 1.56 V.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.8: (a) An Ag+/Ag, Zn2+/Zn electrochemical cell, (b) The difference between +0.80 V and -0.76 V is +1.56 V (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.8).

blocks.title: Standard cell potential
blocks.text: E cell = E standard of the more positive half-cell (where reduction occurs) minus E standard of the more negative half-cell (where oxidation occurs).
